claims.claim: Planar two-exit instances admit a cyclic two-gate decomposition. Let the exits be p,q and let B=N(p)∩N(q). Every component of G−({p,q}∪B) is adjacent to at most two vertices of B; when |B|≥3, those two are consecutive in the cyclic order of B around the exits.
claims.evidence: For k=|B|≥3, the embedded K_{2,k} skeleton is 2-connected and has k faces. Its facial-boundary lengths sum to 4k, while every boundary has length at least four, so every face is a 4-cycle p-b_i-q-b_{i+1}-p. A connected component disjoint from the skeleton lies in one face, hence can meet only its two consecutive B-vertices. For k≤2 the bound is immediate. Equivalently, attachment to three B-vertices would produce a K_{3,3} minor.
claims.witness: The checker examined 51,158 components across every planar labeled graph on three through six vertices and found zero components attached to more than two common neighbors.
claims.search_method: Independent Euler-formula, facial-boundary, and planar-minor proof; exhaustive finite validation without web access.

claims.claim: There is a linear-time classification when the exits have the same independent neighborhood. After deleting a possible irrelevant edge pq, suppose N(p)=N(q)=B and B is independent. The fugitive wins exactly when (i) s∈{p,q}∪B, (ii) s has a neighbor in B, or (iii) s has a neighbor w having two distinct neighbors in B.
claims.evidence: Each listed condition supplies the stated immediate strategy. Conversely, when all fail, after the first move the current outside vertex sees at most one of its component's at most two gates. Nemesis can prepare a gate by deleting one of its two exit edges before Fugitive can enter it. Upon entry she deletes the other edge. Independence of B forces the next non-exit move into an outside component having at most one additional gate, which can be prepared immediately after that move. This invariant prevents entry into any gate with two live exit edges, and finite edge deletion forces a Nemesis win. The predicates are computable by adjacency scans.
claims.witness: Exact minimax over all 1,190 planar promised graphs through six vertices covered 7,010 starting positions and produced zero classification mismatches.
claims.search_method: Direct strategy and invariant audit, followed by exhaustive exact surviving-edge minimax on all small promised instances.

claims.claim: Two broader target-relevant subclasses are linearly solvable: (a) the graph induced by regular vertices is a forest, with arbitrary degrees; or (b) every regular vertex has degree at most three, with arbitrary exit degrees.
claims.evidence: After handling an exit start and deleting pq, replacing each regular-exit incidence by a unique pendant exit gives a state-by-state correspondence: regular moves, deletable edges, immediate exit moves, and post-deletion exit-connectivity all agree. In case (a), every relevant transformed component is a tree; in case (b), the entire transformed graph has maximum degree at most three. The source's respective linear-time algorithms therefore apply, and the transformation is linear-size.
claims.witness: The reduction maps every edge vx with exit x to one distinct leaf edge vx_{v,x}; a path from a regular position to an original exit exists exactly when the corresponding transformed path reaches one of these leaves.
claims.search_method: Independent reduction audit against the source game semantics and the source's tree/maximum-degree-three theorem; small-state checks also found no component-discard mismatch.

claims.claim: Internal-edge deletions are essential even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits: constraining Nemesis to delete only exit-incident edges can change the winner. Let the exits be p,q, the start be s, and the other vertices be x,a,b, with edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ax,xs,ab. Nemesis wins the original game, but the Fugitive wins under that restriction.
claims.evidence: In the unrestricted game the forced move s→x is answered by deleting xa, immediately separating x from both exits. Under the restriction, the first deletion damages either a or b. If it damages b, a retains two exit edges; if it damages a, Fugitive moves through a and either exits there or, after its second exit edge is deleted, crosses ab to the still-fresh b. One deletion cannot then destroy both b-exit edges.
claims.search_method: Complete move-case analysis plus exact minimax and integer segment-intersection verification.

claims.claim: Nemesis is not invariant under edge subdivision, even on planar simple trees with exactly two exits. With exits p,q, start s, and regular vertex a, the graph with edges sa,ap,aq is a Fugitive win, while subdividing sa once with a new regular vertex x makes it a Nemesis win. More generally, replacing r parallel sa edges by the r paths s-x_i-a fails to preserve the winner for every r≥1.
claims.evidence: In the original graph or multigraph, Fugitive moves s→a and one deletion cannot remove both ap and aq. In the subdivided graph, whenever Fugitive enters x_i from s, Nemesis deletes x_i-a before the next move; after a return to s or entry into an already cut branch, she deletes another surviving x_j-a. Thus Fugitive never reaches a, and after r such deletions the current component has no exit. The r=1 pair consists of planar simple trees; every path-bundle graph is planar and simple.
claims.witness: Exact minimax confirmed original_Fwin=1 and subdivided_Fwin=0 independently for every r from 1 through 6; the invariant proves all r≥1.
claims.search_method: General invariant proof plus exact finite-state checks for the first six multiplicities.

claims.claim: The binary-escape-tree condition is not necessary even for planar simple graphs with exactly two exits. A seven-vertex counterexample has exits p,q, start s, regular vertices a,b,c,z, and edges pa,pb,qa,qb,ab,az,bz,bc,cz,cs.
claims.evidence: After s→c, deletion of bc is answered by c→z, where the edge-disjoint a- and b-gate triples ensure one intact route. Any other first deletion permits c→b; Fugitive exits directly unless both b-exit edges are the first two deletions, in which case ab and both a-exit edges remain. After exit splitting, pruning removes none of a,b,c,z. Root s is impossible because it has one neighbor. Root c must use b and z as children because s cannot be a regular leaf; then z would require both a and the already-used b as children, contradicting that the subgraph is a tree.
claims.witness: Exact output: Fwin=1, tree_condition=0, drawing_crossings=0 for the supplied integer embedding.
claims.search_method: Exhaustive deletion-case proof, structural binary-tree exclusion, exact minimax, and integer planarity check.

claims.claim: The seven-vertex binary-escape-tree counterexample is vertex-minimal: no planar simple Nemesis instance with exactly two exits and at most six vertices has a Fugitive-winning regular start that fails the binary-escape-tree condition after the source's exit splitting and pruning.
claims.evidence: The exact enumeration covers every loopless labeled edge subset for n=3,4,5,6 with exits fixed as 0,1. For at most six vertices, Kuratowski obstructions are exhaustively represented by K5, K5 with one subdivided edge, and K3,3. Every exit-connected regular start was evaluated by exact minimax. Exit splitting, iterative pruning, component retention, and rooted full-binary-tree existence were then checked combinatorially. No winning start failed the condition.
claims.witness: Reproduced totals: 33,166 planar graphs; 125,655 exit-connected regular starts; 111,587 Fugitive-winning starts; zero winning tree-condition failures. The seven-vertex witness is independently rejected by the same tree test.
claims.search_method: Complete labeled-graph enumeration with exact Kuratowski testing, exact game recurrence, and exhaustive degree-constrained tree-subgraph testing.

claims.claim: An exact recurrence gives PSPACE membership and an O*(8^n) planar algorithm, although not a polynomial classification. For deleted-edge set D and current regular vertex v, W(D,v) holds iff some surviving move vw reaches an exit or, for every surviving edge e Nemesis might delete, w remains connected to an exit and W(D∪{e},w) holds.
claims.evidence: The existential move followed by universal deletion exactly matches the move order, while the connectivity conjunct implements Nemesis's immediate terminal win. Each recursive call adds one edge to D, giving depth at most m and polynomial space under depth-first evaluation. Memoization has at most n·2^m states with polynomial transition work. For a planar simple graph, m≤3n−6, hence O*(2^m)=O*(8^n). This is exponential and does not supply the target's requested classification.
claims.witness: The persisted checker evaluates the equivalent recurrence over surviving-edge masks, with all successor masks strictly smaller, and uses it for the complete six-vertex census and all stated witnesses.
claims.search_method: Independent quantifier/order audit, termination and state-count analysis, plus exact bottom-up implementation.

target_evidence: The source target requires either a polynomial-time classification for all planar simple two-exit instances or a matching hardness result. The draft expressly states that it obtained neither. Its verified decomposition, exact promised-class classification, two additional linear-time subclasses, counterexamples, minimality result, and exponential baseline are material target-relevant progress but leave arbitrary planar two-boundary pieces unresolved. Therefore PARTIAL is accurate and the target is not fully resolved.
